metaData.originalTitle: Vector RAG Isn’t Enough — I Built a Context Graph Layer for Multi-Agent Memory
metaData.title: Vector RAG Isn’t Enough — I Built a Context Graph Layer for Multi-Agent Memory
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a context graph layer for multi-agent memory that outperforms raw history dumps and vector-only RAG on join queries by storing facts as entities and relationships, achieving 88.9% accuracy at 26.9 tokens per query.
metaData.summary: The author describes building a multi-agent system where agents frequently fail to recall decisions made by other agents, even when full transcripts are available. After identifying the issue as a structural retrieval problem rather than a token compression or staleness issue, they propose a context graph architecture that stores facts as (subject, predicate, object) triples in a NetworkX graph, enabling multi-hop traversal for join queries. A deterministic benchmark with 18 graded queries across five scenarios compares three architectures: raw history dump (61.1% accuracy, 490.9 tokens/query), vector-only RAG using TF-IDF (50.0%, 75.9 tokens/query), and the context graph (88.9%, 26.9 tokens/query). The graph wins both accuracy and efficiency, with the largest gap on join queries (80% vs 20%). The article also discusses two identified bugs—entity vocabulary mismatch and stale fact retrieval—and their fixes, which are critical for production use.

mainPoints.point: Flat memory stores (raw transcripts and vector RAG) have a structural blind spot for join queries that require combining two separately stated facts.
mainPoints.explanation: No single chunk or embedding contains both pieces of information, so similarity search cannot produce the correct answer regardless of model quality. This is the core problem the context graph solves.

mainPoints.point: The context graph stores facts as entities and typed relationships, enabling graph traversal to answer multi-hop questions.
mainPoints.explanation: By filtering out distractors and writing only structured triples into a NetworkX multigraph, the system can walk from entity to entity along relationships like DEPENDS_ON or ASSIGNED_TO, retrieving combined information that flat stores miss.

mainPoints.point: The benchmark is fully deterministic (no LLM calls, no random state) to isolate architectural differences, and the results show clear superiority of the graph: 88.9% vs 61.1% vs 50.0% accuracy.
mainPoints.explanation: Using rule-based extraction, TF-IDF vectorizer, and substring matching for grading, the test is reproducible byte-for-byte. The graph's token efficiency (26.9 vs 490.9 tokens/query) is an additional practical advantage.

mainPoints.point: Two production-critical bugs—entity vocabulary mismatch and stale fact retrieval—were discovered and fixed, highlighting real engineering challenges.
mainPoints.explanation: Graph nodes must be linked to query language via aliases, and fact supersession must be explicitly handled (old edges removed when a predicate is restated) to avoid returning outdated information with full confidence.

keyQuotes: Multi-agent systems lose cross-agent decisions because flat transcripts and vector search both have a structural blind spot — not just a noise problem.
The context graph wins on accuracy and uses about 18x fewer tokens per query than the raw dump. That is not a tradeoff—it is a win on both axes.
If you are shipping anything like this, handling fact supersession is not optional. It is the exact line between building a reliable memory layer and building a major liability.

relatedArticles.title: Embeddings Aren’t Magic: The Predictable Failure Modes of RAG Retrieval
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically debunks the magic of embeddings in RAG systems, demonstrating through reproducible experiments that embeddings excel at public vocabulary tasks but predictably fail on enterprise-specific terms, negation, magnitudes, and answer relevance, advocating for upstream filtering over stronger models.

relatedArticles.title: Stop Treating AI Memory Like a Search Problem
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article critiques the conventional 'store-and-retrieve' approach to AI memory, proposing a lifecycle-based system with decay, contradiction detection, confidence scoring, compression, and expiry to manage memory like a human brain rather than a static archive.

relatedArticles.title: How to Build a Self-Learning RAG System with Knowledge Reflection
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This tutorial shows you how to build a self-learning RAG system that synthesizes connections between documents during ingestion, creating retrievable reflection artifacts that make the knowledge base smarter over time.

relatedArticles.title: A Guide to Context Engineering for LLMs
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A comprehensive guide to context engineering that explains why more context can degrade LLM performance and outlines four core strategies—Write, Select, Compress, and Isolate—to optimize model outputs.

relatedArticles.title: Memory and Dreaming for Self-Learning Agents
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic introduces Memory and Dreaming, two new primitives for its Managed Agents API, enabling agents to achieve continuous self-learning by managing their own knowledge in a file system-like structure and asynchronously curating that knowledge to improve over time.

relatedArticles.title: Building an Evaluation Harness for Production AI Agents: A 12-Metric Framework From 100+ Deployments
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a comprehensive 12-metric evaluation framework for production AI agents, distilled from over 100 enterprise deployments, covering retrieval, generation, agent behavior, and production health.

relatedArticles.title: Your ReAct Agent Is Wasting 90% of Its Retries — Here’s How to Stop It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article identifies a critical architectural flaw in ReAct-style LLM agents where hallucinated tool names waste the majority of retry budgets, and proposes three structural fixes—error taxonomy, per-tool circuit breakers, and deterministic tool routing—to eliminate this waste and improve production reliability.

relatedArticles.title: Hybrid Search and Re-Ranking in Production RAG
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a production-grade approach to improving RAG retrieval quality by combining hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) with cross-encoder re-ranking and metadata filtering, supported by real-world evaluation metrics.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing workspace agents in ChatGPT
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI introduces workspace agents, a new class of shared, long-running AI agents within ChatGPT for business teams, designed to automate complex workflows, integrate with organizational tools, and operate under enterprise-grade controls.

relatedArticles.title: Agents that remember: introducing Agent Memory
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cloudflare announces the private beta of Agent Memory, a managed service that provides AI agents with persistent, context-aware memory by extracting and retrieving knowledge from conversations, solving the problem of context rot without overfilling the context window.
